newsitem.title: FRANCE: Algeria assembly backs ambitious three-year plan.
newsitem.headline: Algeria assembly backs ambitious three-year plan.

text.p: Algeria's fractious three-party government coalition buried their differences on Sunday to push through parliament an ambitious programme of jobs, growth and housing by the year 2000.

In a test of Algeria's new democracy, enshrined in its first multi-party parliament elected last June 5, the 380-seat assembly wound up nearly a week of acrimonious debate to vote on the government's three-year agenda.
The 1997-2000 plan targets creating 1.2 million jobs, building 800,000 homes, and lifting Gross Domestic Product growth to seven percent from an average four percent.
It also envisages cutting Algeria's foreign debt to $26 billion in the year 2000 from the $32 billion it totalled at the end of 1996.
The house adopted the plan by 245 votes to 72, with 26 abstaining, said the official Algerian news agency APS.

Opposition parties and some coalition deputies criticised the programme outlined by Prime Minister Ahmed Ouyahia for what they said was a lack of credible figures. But in the end, dissident coalition MPs rallied to keep the government intact.

Independent analysts also questioned whether the programme, one plank of which is heavy investment, could be achieved without significant change in security in Algeria. Outside of the energy sector, they said, there appeared little foreign interest in investing in the North African country.

About 60,000 people have died since early 1992 in Algeria's conflict which officials blame on Moslem fundamentalists. In the past two months alone, more than 1,000 people are reported to have been killed.
Some of the programmes aimed at soaking up some of the jobless involve work on renewing road and rail infrastructure outside of cities.
"Much of that sort of work is constrained by (lack of) security in much of the country," one analyst said last week.
Algerian officials have blamed poverty, lack of jobs and shortage of accommodation for driving many young people into the ranks of Moslem fundamentalists.

An estimated 2.2 million mostly young people are officially out of work -- 28 percent of the workforce. Many live in cramped, overcrowded apartments with little or no hope of marriage without a job and prospects of their own dwelling. Officials put the housing shortage at one million units.

Economic reforms which have increased Algeria's foreign reserves to $6.4 billion and won plaudits from international financial bodies, like the World Bank and International Monetary Fund, have added to internal strains.

Many Algerians fear privatisation will lead to mass layoffs from firms grown bloated and hugely inefficient over nearly three decades of centralised management which Algeria has been trying to change to a market economy.

European analysts say fear of adding to the jobless has effectively hobbled the two-year-old privatisation programme on which President Liamine Zeroual had pinned hopes for revitalising part of the economy.

The prime minister told the house last week there was cause for "legitimate optimism" with growth based on annual total exports of $17 billion in the year 2000, including $2 billion from non-hydrocarbon exports.

He angrily rejected criticism from members of the junior partner to the coalition, the Movement of a Peaceful Society (MPS), who joined opposition deputies to criticise parts of the government programme.
The MPS and the National Liberation Front (FLN) are junior members in the government dominated by the National Democratic Rally. The three control 287 of the assembly's 380 seats.

"You have said 'government of liars'. You had two members in the previous cabinet and seven positions in the current one," Ouyahia reminded an MPS deputy during the televised debate, which gave many of Algeria's 29 million people their first sight of open political infighting.
